author: anglinb
body:
Forking required an idle chat, so branching off a long-running turn meant waiting for it or interrupting it. A running chat is now forkable: the fork branches from the **last completed turn**, and the source keeps running untouched.

### Why not copy the in-flight turn

Copying it verbatim would hand the fork a conversation head whose tool calls have no results yet. So `EventStore.forkChat` takes `atLastCompletedTurn` and trims the copy at the last `result` entry — or `interrupted`, which is what Claude emits for a cancelled turn.

- `agent.ts` — the `"Chat must be idle before forking"` throw is gone; it passes `atLastCompletedTurn` when the chat has an active or draining turn.
- `event-store.ts` — new `findLastCompletedTurnEnd`; entry resolution moved above the first write, so a refused fork leaves no half-built chat behind. Sidebar previews are re-derived from the trimmed copy via `summarizeForkedTranscript` (inheriting them from the source record would advertise the prompt the fork deliberately left behind), and the turn count drops the turn in flight.
- `read-models.ts` — `canForkChat` allows busy chats that have a `lastTurnEndedAt`. A chat still inside its very first turn has no settled branch point and stays unforkable.

Composes with the existing media-URL retargeting on copy.

### Known gap

The native session fork still happens when the fork is **first prompted**, not when it is created — `pendingForkSessionToken` is consumed then. A fork prompted after the source's turn lands therefore resumes a session that contains that turn: the fork's visible transcript stops at the branch point, but the harness's context won't. Pinning the branch point needs Claude's `resumeSessionAt` (our entries already carry the message uuid in `messageId`); codex's `thread/fork` takes only a thread id, so it would be Claude-only. Left for a follow-up.

### Testing

`bun run check` clean. Full `bun test` green (1704 tests). New coverage: a mid-turn fork trims the copy and survives a reload; a first-turn fork is refused without creating a chat; the sidebar affordance appears for a busy chat only once a turn has completed.

🌸 Shipped with [Kanna](https://kanna.sh) — an open-source workspace for all your coding agents. Written by `claude/opus`.

author: fx
body:
Documentation only. Five change documents planning work, and the spec amendments that own the behaviour they implement. No implementation is included, and every `## Tasks` checkbox is deliberately unticked — this repository writes and reviews a change document before the code, and implements it separately.

Everything here came out of testing the merged server against live Sonarr 4.0.19.2979, Radarr 6.3.0.10514, and Prowlarr 2.5.2.5491 instances, prompted by two problems: `arr_config_reconcile` had to be excluded from a host's configuration by hand because llama.cpp could not compile its published input schema into a decoding grammar, and tool results were large enough that harnesses were writing them to disk and reading them back rather than holding them in context.

## What was measured

| observation | figure |
|---|---|
| `arr_config_observe` indexers/prowlarr at `detail: "full"`, `pageSize: 1` | 1,044,260 bytes — and identical at `pageSize: 10` |
| the same call at `detail: "summary"` | 778 bytes |
| of that megabyte, `data.schema.templates` (624 entries) | 1,043,460 bytes, against 1,366 bytes of records |
| `tools/list` | 165,839 bytes, of which 135,490 is output schemas |
| that 135,490, split | 59,302 envelope (fifteen near-identical copies) / 76,188 data |
| `arr_library_query`, 25 movies at default detail | 18,296 bytes, roughly 730 per record |
| summed `maxLength` + `maxItems` per published input schema | `arr_config_reconcile` 10,270; next highest `arr_import_inspect` 885 |

The full-detail form of a provider record turned out to differ from the summary form by exactly one key — it adds `"fields": []` — because every one of that record's 37 fields is withheld at both levels. So the megabyte buys an empty array.

## The changes

**0016 — Bounded Provider Schema Observation.** `arr_config_observe` stops returning the instance's provider template catalogue. Nothing reads it: reconciliation re-reads the schema route itself via `readSchemaFingerprint`, and the catalogue's only caller-facing purpose is provider creation, which the server refuses outright.

**0017 — Grammar-Compilable Input Schemas.** Published input schemas stop declaring string length bounds. A host compiling one into a decoding grammar expands a `maxLength` once per admissible character, which is why one tool at 10,270 failed while everything at or below 885 compiled. The bounds stay in validation and move into the published root's description, the same bargain 0015 struck for cross-property constraints. Lowering the numbers would not have worked: all three long bounds at 512 still leaves that tool above a known-good 885.

**0018 — Bounded Tool Listing.** Published output schemas are broadened to the four top-level keys and `applications[].data`, and each payload's selectable **leaf paths** are generated as documentation instead. This does for output what 0015 did for input. A path list runs roughly 300 bytes per view against `arr_library_query`'s 37,444, and it is the form a projection is actually written in.

**0019 — Selected Result Fields.** A collection query may name which parts of each payload to return, as dot-paths relative to `data` with arrays traversing element-wise. Projection happens after the envelope has been validated, so a projected result is provably a subset of a conforming one. Both input bounds are derived from 0018's inventory rather than picked, so a bound can never refuse a projection naming exactly what the tool advertises.

**0020 — Withdraw the Configuration Write Surface.** `arr_config_reconcile` and the roughly 5,000 lines serving it are removed; configuration becomes read-only. Of its nine declared intents, three were refused unconditionally with `<intent> is declared but not implemented yet`, discoverable only by calling the tool. The substantive remainder is provider management, which this project has decided not to support for now, and what would survive that is renaming a quality profile, renaming a tag, and Prowlarr sync levels.

## Spec changes

**Tool Contracts** gains the two publication rules (no published string length bound, no published intent the server refuses unconditionally) and the projection contract, and loses `arr_config_reconcile` from the tool list. The transient-secret requirements move out, because with that tool gone no tool accepts a secret and nothing could satisfy them.

**Configuration Reconciliation** is restructured to separate the surface the server exposes from the one it does not. The observation requirements stand as current; the reconciliation requirements are retained under `## Retained Design — The Withdrawn Write Surface`, clearly marked as describing nothing currently implemented. They encode real design work — the scoped read-modify-write, explicit removal, staleness on a changed provider schema, secrets that never retain a value — and the decision is "not for now", not "never".

## Implementation order

The dependency graph is `0016 → none`, `0017 → 0015, 0020`, `0018 → 0015`, `0019 → 0017, 0018`, `0020 → none`. Numbering is creation order and does not match priority, as with 0011 through 0014 before it. Recommended: **0020 first** — it is a deletion that shrinks everything downstream and removes the live grammar failure along with the tool that caused it — then 0016, then 0018 → 0019, with 0017 any time after 0020. 0017 is preventive rather than corrective once 0020 has landed, and is still worth having: nothing else stops the bound being reintroduced, and 0019 adds a bounded path array to five tools immediately.

## Review

Codex reviewed this branch to convergence: 4 blocking findings on pass 1, 0 on pass 2. All four were internal contradictions in the plan rather than defects in what it plans — a generator sequenced to read bounds that had already been stripped, a restatement attached to variant documentation that two plain-object inputs do not produce, two mandated bounds with no stated value, and an ordering conflict between 0016 and 0020 that neither declared. Sweeping the last as a class found a further undeclared dependency in 0019, now fixed and synchronized across both index files.

### Closing note, non-blocking

One open question is recorded rather than answered: whether `arr_capabilities` should accept a projection. Its report is already bounded by its own detail level, so the case is weaker than for the five collection queries; it is out of 0019's scope, which under 0018 also means it publishes no path inventory.

author: lukehha
body:
## What the audit found

I audited the build system at `e251ac75` against the canonical documents and
the source. Four of the five `B-PROJECT` rows are complete; `B-PROJECT-05` was
the one **ready** row, and it turned out to name a real, currently-observable
defect rather than a speculative API.

The driver resolves a workspace into a package source-root graph, and the build
path passes that graph to `Frontend::analyze` so `#include <alias/unit>`
resolves through each package's direct aliases. The LSP does not. It reads the
manifest itself:

```cpp
const ManifestDiscoveryResult discovery = discoverProjectManifest(...);
const ManifestLoadResult manifest = loadProjectManifest(*discovery.path);
configurationFlags = manifest.manifest->build().defines;
if (const ProjectProfile *profile = manifest.manifest->findProfile("dev")) { ... }
```

and then analyzes with five arguments:

```cpp
.analyze(*filePath, source, {standardLibrary.prelude},
         request.sourceOverrides, {standardLibrary.root})
```

`analyze`'s sixth parameter is `packageSourceRoots`, which therefore defaults to
empty. **Every package include that `gti check` resolves fails to resolve in the
editor**, and no amount of manifest reading fixes it, because the graph is a
property of the workspace closure rather than of any single manifest.

That is the weakness this row exists to close: consumers have no supported way
to obtain the driver's resolution, so they reimplement a subset of it and drift.

## What this implements

`include/gti/driver/project_facts.h` publishes the resolved project as
read-only values:

- the workspace root and whether a `[workspace]` table declared it;
- the resolved package closure — identity, membership, manifest/package/source
  roots, selectability, git provenance, and direct alias edges;
- **the package source-root graph**, the fact that cannot be reconstructed from
  one manifest;
- the selected package's declared profiles and targets;
- package-level configuration flags and the profile a command selects when none
  is named;
- `analysisConfiguration(profile, target, runtimeProfile)`, assembled exactly as
  the build path assembles it;
- the workspace-graph model identity, which a build plan extends with its
  configuration flags and bindgen imports.

Native settings, output layout, and cache policy are build concerns and are
deliberately absent.

`resolveProjectFacts` answers for the project containing a directory;
`projectFactsFromWorkspace` describes a workspace the caller already resolved,
so nothing resolves twice.

### Read-only means read-only

Resolution runs no native tool, no git process, and no build, and creates no
directories. It uses the same dependency policy as `gti metadata`
(`{.allowAcquisition = false}`).

Worth stating explicitly, because the opposite choice looks tempting: I did
**not** use `requireLock = false`. That flag reads like "don't be strict", but
in `workspace.cpp` it selects the *fetch* path and shells out to git. Using it
would have made a read-only facts query execute processes. With the metadata
policy, stored checkouts stay checksum-verified, `gti.lock` remains the coverage
authority, and an unmaterialized or unlocked dependency is reported as a
diagnostic instead of being acquired.

## Scope

The row says it "does not integrate the LSP, fetch, or build", so the LSP is
untouched here — consuming these facts with dirty buffers authoritative is
`T-LSP-04`, which this unblocks. I updated the architecture doc to state the
current LSP divergence plainly rather than leaving the old aspirational wording.

## Tests

Library tests in `tests/project_tests.cpp`:

- a declared workspace with a member and a path dependency: closure, selection,
  membership, alias edges, source roots, declared source-root override;
- the source-root graph specifically, including the dependency's canonical root;
- profiles, default profile name, per-profile execution profile, configuration
  flags, and analysis configuration for both declared and undeclared profiles;
- targets and their kinds;
- **agreement with the build path** — the same project's `ProjectBuildPlan`
  reports the same source-root count and configuration flags, and its model
  identity extends the facts' identity;
- `projectFactsFromWorkspace` matching `resolveProjectFacts`;
- read-only proof: no build directory is created;
- failures: discovery, malformed manifest (diagnostics, no partial facts), and
  unknown `--package` selection;
- a standalone package with a path dependency, covering `Dependency` membership
  and unselectability.

`tests/driver_library_smoke.cpp` exercises the surface too. That smoke runs both
in-tree and against the **installed** package, so it proves the header ships and
the symbol is exported rather than only that it compiles in-tree.

## Notes

- `VERSION` → 0.323.0 (minor: new published driver surface).
- Two of my initial assertions were wrong and the code was right — a workspace
  member is selectable, and a build plan's model identity extends rather than
  equals the workspace identity. I corrected the tests and sharpened the header
  doc instead of loosening the assertions.

author: 00o-sh
body:
Stacked on #123. The blocker named there, removed.

## The problem

The sidecar turns intents into chat command **strings** — `start` becomes `/new name --safe` — and everything in that string is split on whitespace.

A title with spaces would arrive as arguments. A title reading `refactor auth --dangerous` would arrive as a **flag**. That is the same mistake `answer`-as-an-ordinal exists to avoid: a string that looks bounded and is not.

## The fix

Prose travels **beside** the command, never inside it:

```
POST /api/command  { command: "/new job", title: "refactor auth", brief: "…" }
```

`toCommandLine()` builds the line, `commandMeta()` picks out the prose, and they sit next to each other in `sidecar.js` deliberately — split across a module is how one of them acquires a parameter the other has never heard of.

There is a test asserting the line is **byte-identical** with and without a title, including one whose text ends in `--dangerous`.

## One definition of acceptable text

`src/core/text.js` holds `cleanText()`, used by the protocol validator **and** by the HTTP route.

That route is reachable by anything holding the hub token, not only by the sidecar that already validated — so it validates again, with the same function. Two doors into one store checking separately is exactly the shape of the `?token=fwk_` bug, where the Worker and the Durable Object extracted credentials differently and the disagreement failed **open**.

`TITLE_MAX` and `BRIEF_MAX` live there too, so a `60` in the route and a `60` in the protocol cannot become two numbers that merely agree today.

## Three smaller decisions

- **A supplied title is pinned.** Without `titlePinned` the transcript hook replaces it a few seconds later and the field looks like it silently did not save.
- **Only on a fresh start.** A resume must not carry these, or a later caller could quietly rewrite a title somebody set deliberately.
- **The title is not logged.** The sidecar logs the command line, which by construction no longer contains it. A person's sentence about their own work has no reason to sit in a journal the whole box can read.

## What typecheck caught that the tests did not

Four gaps: the inline `@param` object on `#launch`, the `Ctx` typedef, and a tuple that inferred `(string|number)[]`. The threading through `start` → `#launch` is exactly where a hand-written change would have compiled and silently dropped the field.

`./scripts/verify.sh` — ALL GREEN.

## Next

App UI, the kind editor, then the Foundation Models / Gemini Nano calls.

author: copilot
body:
GitHub Pages serves project sites at `https://arundamo.github.io/Evroadlabs/`, but `base: './'` in `vite.config.ts` generates relative asset URLs that break under this subpath — the browser resolves them against the root, causing 404s for all JS/CSS chunks and the page to not load.

## Change

```ts
// before
base: './',

// after
base: '/Evroadlabs/',
```

This makes Vite emit absolute asset paths prefixed with `/Evroadlabs/`, matching how GitHub Pages serves the site.

body:
前日比の基準を「前日の残高」に変え、任意の日の残高を引ける API を足す。

## 理由

`prev_value` は `いまの残高 × 前日終値` だった（`web/app.py`）。残高は**数量そのもの**なので、両日を同じ残高で評価すると入出庫が打ち消し合い、`day_change` は価格が動いたぶんしか表せない。今日 1 BTC 入金しても前日比には出てこない。

実台帳で見ると、直近30日で **10 資産の数量が動いていた**（BTC 0.7814→0.8811、SOL 8.0074→0.0074、USDC +3,231 など）。この定義ではその増減が丸ごと落ちる。

## 変更

- `prev_value = 前日（prev_date 時点）の残高 × 前営業日の終値`。`day_change` は**その日に資産が実際にどれだけ増減したか**になり、`/api/portfolio-history` の前日の点との差と一致する
- `prev_balance` を応答に追加。価格変動だけが要る利用側は `prev_balance × (price − prev_price)` で従来の値を作れる
- 前日にあって当日に無い資産（その日に全部売った・送り出した）も `balance="0"` で載せる。落とすと受け取った側だけが増えて、売却日に見かけの利益が出る。`asset_count` / `priced_count` / `unpriced` はこの行を数えない（翌日には消える）
- 資産ごとに `prev_date` が違いうるので、残高もその資産の `prev_date` 時点のものを使う（日付の違う残高と価格を掛けない）

追加リクエストは発生しない。前日残高は `Ledger.balances(until=...)` の SQL 1 本で、CoinGecko は増えない。

## `GET /api/balances`（新規）

指定日の終わり時点の残高を**数量だけ**返す。価格を引かないので CoinGecko を叩かず SQL 1 本。

```
GET /api/balances?as_of=2026-07-29&scope=total
→ {"as_of": "2026-07-29", "scope": "total", "assets": [{"asset": "BTC", "balance": "0.78142..."}, ...]}
```

`scope` は `/api/portfolio-history` と同じ書式（`total` / `account:<表示名>` / `asset:<SYM>`）。解釈は `_scope_filters` に共通化した。2 つの日付で叩いて引き算すれば、**価格変動と切り分けた持ち高の増減**（1週間差・30日差）が出せる。評価額の推移が要るなら `portfolio-history`、数量の推移が要るならこちら。

サービストークンで読める（`Depends(get_db_path_read)`）。読み取りルートは 5 本 → 6 本。

## 検証

- `core.portfolio.balances_as_of()` が `daily_balances` の同じ日の値と**完全に一致**することを実台帳（38資産）で確認。7日前・30日前とも一致。最初はゼロ残高の扱いで食い違っていたので、日次系列と同じくゼロを落とすよう揃えた
- HTTP 経由で `as_of=2026-07-29` が 38 資産、`scope=asset:BTC` が 1 件、不正な日付が 422
- 実台帳で `_summary` を通し、`prev_balance` が入ること・基準日を30日前にずらすと数量の増減が `day_change` に乗ることを確認（BTC +0.0996、SOL −8.0、USDC +3,231.7）
- テスト 606 件通過（新規 9 件: 前日残高ベースの前日比・当日ゼロの資産・残高 API・`balances_as_of` と日次系列の一致）

## 利用側（Asset Summary）

AS はこの `prev_value` をそのまま引き算するので、暗号資産の入出庫・売買も前日比に入り、AS 内の銘柄と定義が揃う（AS 側 PR で `prev_balance` を「その版の CS である印」として扱う）。返さない旧 CS 相手のときだけ従来どおり相場変動のみになる。

`docs/api.md` の §3・§4 と新エンドポイント §9 を更新済み。

author: luislipinski
yosriady
body:
Follows up the codex P2 threads on #367 (connector attribution for `eip1193Fallback` captures).

## Problem

With `wagmi: { eip1193Fallback: true }`, request-derived events (imperative `personal_sign`, `eth_sendTransaction`, batches) took their `providerName` from the registry, which for a provider that was never announced falls back to flag sniffing. Hook-driven events from the same connection use the connector name. A custom or embedded connector whose provider exposes no recognised flag therefore split one wallet's activity between `Injected Provider` and the connector's name.

## Fix

- `WagmiEventHandler` hands `_wrapWagmiProvider` a resolver bound to the connector whose `getProvider` resolved to the wrapped provider. The name is what the hook path emits for that connector (live WalletConnect peer for a WalletConnect connector, the connector's own name otherwise), so the two paths cannot disagree. Bound, not "whichever connector is current": a request issued over a previous connector's provider (a retained wallet client) belongs to the wallet that handles it. A provider shared by two connectors is re-bound when the new connector's resolution lands (one microtask for an injected connector); a request inside that gap keeps the previous label.
- `FormoAnalytics._wrapWagmiProvider` records the resolver via a new `EvmProviderRegistry.rememberAttribution`.
- `infoFor` reads the resolver on each lookup and prefers it over sniffing; a supplied name without an rdns keeps the sniffed rdns; a supplied name that is the generic transport name still gets the live peer; EIP-6963 announcement metadata still wins. The resolver is read on each request start, so a WalletConnect peer that resolves later still names the wallet.
- `WagmiConnector` now types `rdns?: string | readonly string[]`. Only a single string rdns is passed through; a connector listing several does not say which one its provider is, so the registry keeps the sniffed rdns.
- `EvmRequestTracker` now resolves the attribution once when a request begins and holds it for every status of that request, receipt poll included (the same pattern the chain snapshot already used). Two connectors sharing one provider, or a session change during the receipt poll, no longer split one operation between two wallet names.
- Bundle budget raised from 58.75 to 59 KB (size is 58.8 kB; the same 0.25 KB step #376 took).

## Tests

- `test/wagmi/hybridCapture.spec.ts`: imperative captures are named after the connector (fails on `main` with `Injected Provider`); connector rdns propagates, sniffed rdns is kept when the connector has none or lists several; a connector switch to a new provider re-attributes; the same provider taken over by a different connector re-attributes; a switch while a signature prompt is open keeps one name for requested and confirmed; a switch mid-transaction keeps one name through started, broadcasted and the polled receipt; a request in the same tick as a connector switch keeps the previous label and the shared provider is rebound after; a request over a previous connector's provider keeps that connector's name (the provider A/B isolation test now asserts names as well as chains); a branded WalletConnect-backed connector keeps its own name as on the hook path; a one-element rdns list counts as one value.
- `test/evm/EvmProviderRegistry.spec.ts`: supplied attribution, sniffed-rdns fallback, resolver read live, peer replacement only for the generic name, resolver that yields nothing or throws, forgetting, and 6963 precedence.
- `pnpm test`: 1198 passing. `pnpm lint` clean. e2e against `../examples` with this build: sweep 13/13, behaviours 35/35, SDK harness 15/15, browser suites (SDK + examples) all checks passed. Codex (gpt-5.5, high) review, five rounds, iterated until no major findings; every minor and nit addressed. The four codex-connector threads on this PR (snapshot per request; array-valued rdns; same-tick switch; branded connector peer rule) are fixed in 790febd, c3478e7 and b5d09dc and answered inline.

author: denisvmedia
body:
The twelfth family off `[]string` under #2315, the largest, and the one a name cost the most. It also fixes #2404.

## What this changes

`ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` needs the type, the nullability, the default and
everything else a column declares. A planner handed a **name** recovered them by
finding the table's Go *struct* name and then scanning every field in the schema
for one matching both — a parser artifact reaching into the planner, and a
silent no-op when either half of the match failed.

**Both sides carry, and they have to.** `reverseTableDiffs` swaps the two lists
to build a down migration, so the rollback of a dropped column reads its
definition out of what the *removal* carried. A removed column is absent from
the desired schema by definition, so the comparison describes it from the
catalog through `catalogfield.Field` — moved out of `internal/convert` for
exactly this in #2403.

## The removal carries the column and not its keys — which fixes #2404

Two independent paths recovered a rolled-back column's foreign key:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| the column | the reversal's desired side is built from the database read, which puts the key on the field |
| the constraint comparison | reports the same key as a removal, and the reversal turns it into an addition |

Each is right on its own. Nothing paired them, so the rollback emitted
`ADD CONSTRAINT` **twice**, and PostgreSQL answers the second with
`constraint "..." for relation "..." already exists` — the rollback could not
apply. Measured on master before this change; the regression test asserts the
**count**, because one statement and two both "contain" the constraint.

The forward direction is unaffected, and that was measured too: a *declared*
field carries its own foreign key, and the constraint comparison reports none
for it (`constraintsAdded=[]`), so the column path is the only one that emits it
there.

## Removing the lookup removed a guard with it

The tests caught this, and it is the part most worth reviewing. A diff naming
`app.users` against a schema that declares `reporting.users` must write **no
DDL**, because the statement would apply cleanly to a relation nobody declared —
measured live on PostgreSQL 17.10 and pinned by
`TestPlannerWritesNoDDLForARelationTheSchemaDoesNotDeclare`.

The old field lookup provided that guard as a side effect. The column no longer
needs finding, but the **table** still has to be declared, so the check is now
explicit in the PostgreSQL and MySQL-family planners. Removing it reddens two
tests.

SQLite needed none: it already refuses, with a message naming the table —
`rebuilding table other.users requires its desired definition ... Declare the
table, or drop it instead of changing it`. I added the same guard there first
and it changed no test, so it was dead code; the refusal is pinned instead, and
it is the better answer, since an operator is told what to fix rather than
handed a plan that quietly does less.

## The wire is unchanged

`ColumnChanges.MarshalJSON` emits the name list `format_version: 1` has always
carried, and `cmd/schema`'s JSON structure test still reads `columns_added` back
out of a rendered document as `["email"]` — end to end, not just at the
marshaller.

## Notes for the reviewer

- `findColumn` (SQLite) is gone; it existed to answer the question the change
  now carries.
- Fixtures that asserted `ColumnsAdded` by deep-equality now compare `.Names()`
  where the row is about *which* columns, and carry the definition where the row
  is about what is rendered. `qt.DeepEquals` takes `any`, so those did not fail
  to compile — they failed at runtime.
- One test row is replaced rather than adjusted: "table modification with
  missing field definitions should not generate migration" described a state
  that no longer exists, so it now pins the property it was really about — a
  table diff carrying no change writes no migration.

author: gerrowadat
body:
Fixes #192.

The C's line editor prompts for each line with `] ` and confirms a sent
letter with "Message sent!". The port did neither: silent while typing,
and nothing at all when the letter went.

The prompt is `make_prompt`'s second branch:

```c
    else if (d->str)
      strcpy(prompt, "] ");
```

and the thing worth noticing is what it keys off. Not the connection
state: the *pointer being written to* (comm.c:1008). So it fires for the
improved editor, for `tedit`, for a board post and for the menu's
description editor alike — and it sits above the `CON_PLAYING` test, so a
descriptor at `CON_EXDESC` writing a description gets `] ` and not the
menu's silence. Both paths send it now.

The *first* prompt already worked and nobody had noticed, which is why
this looked like a smaller gap than it was: `Dispatcher.Do`'s tail calls
`prompt()`, and `prompt()` has had the `StateEditing` case since the
editor was written. It was every line after the first that got nothing.

"Message sent!" is `playing_string_cleanup`'s (modify.c:232), and it is
worth more here than in the C. The reference build used for parity
testing is the one whose `store_mail` core-dumps on 64-bit: it takes the
stamp money, says "Message sent!" and delivers nothing. This port actually
delivers, so the line it prints is the only true confirmation either
server gives.

The play suite gets a board post, since this is something a player types
and the board is the only thing on the tour that opens the editor. It
walks the prompt line by line with `doUntil("] ")` rather than the usual
H/M/V barrier — a test that waits for the wrong prompt here hangs.

`make lint` clean, `go test -race -count=1 ./...` green, `make play` has
the three failures it has on `origin/main` and no new ones. `make ci`
could not be run: `actions/setup-go` is being SIGKILLed in the container
on this host, before any repo code is compiled.

## Summary

- make the single public settlement advancement API mutation-only with a Promise<void> return
- migrate the sole genuine checkpoint consumer to the explicit settlement read repository
- add query-observer regression coverage proving provider-page persistence performs no source-head DISTINCT ON scan

## Root cause

The discarded readback scanned about 6.75 million change-cause rows inside every page transaction. The captured pre-fix plan took 7.24 seconds, read about 1.68 GiB of shared buffers, and spilled about 511 MiB to temporary storage to return four source heads.

## Verification

- npm run verify:framework on the final review-adjusted diff
- isolated PostgreSQL 16 focused settlement and atomic-page regression suite
- independent lock-order, fencing, tenant-scope, genuine-consumer, and settlement-invariant review: no blockers

## Rollout

The live import worker is intentionally paused at a durable no-request boundary. After merge, deploy at one persistence slot and measure page persistence/throughput before changing any other capacity guard.

body: ## Summary Fixes the indexer bug where every dirty file was `readFile`'d and sent to Ollama as base64 in `images[]`, causing HTTP 400s on PDF/MP3/DOCX and Node string-limit failures on large PPTX. Adds **extension-based routing before qwen** while keeping the existing flow: walk → hash → dirty → **qwen label+description** → mxbai embed → **one vector per file**. All extractable text goes through qwen — no embed-as-is bypass. ## Routing | Route | Extensions | Processing | |-------|------------|------------| | **docling** | pdf, xlsx, docx, epub, pptx, html, csv | Docling → markdown → qwen **text prompt** (never `images[]`) | | **qwen-text** | txt, sql, js, json, md, xml, conf, css, properties, sh | Read UTF-8 in memory → qwen **text prompt** (never `images[]`) | | **qwen-image** | jpg, jpeg, png | qwen vision `images[]` | | **heic** | heic | temp JPEG (`heif-convert` / ImageMagick) → qwen image; tmp cleaned in `finally` (logged as `qwen-image`) | | **skip** | mp3, wav, svg, certs, bson, bak, no extension, etc. | clear `dirty` without LLM/GPU | ## planIndexWork - **gpu_vision** — any qwen-routed file (docling + qwen-text + images + heic) - **cpu_folders** — folder-only dirty (CPU Xenova folder rollups unchanged) - **none** — skip-only dirty (cleared before planning) ## Infrastructure - **docling-serve** sidecar in `docker-compose.yml` with shared RO NAS mount - Indexer image: `libheif` + ImageMagick for HEIC conversion - `DOCLING_SERVE_URL` env (default `http://docling-serve:5001`) ## Tests (170 passing) - Production extension mix: plain text → `qwen-text`, not text-embed - Skip-only → no GPU - Plain-text-only dirty → `gpu_vision` - Docling / plain text → qwen text without `images[]` - HEIC temp cleanup; Docling client mocked ## Not in scope - No PDF rasterization as primary path - No chunk embeddings - No CPU Xenova path for file contents - Does not merge

author: joielectric
body:
The words all come from the catalogue entry — short description, description, tags, credits, links with TRT — so a description cannot drift from the entry it describes. The only thing a creator styles is the borders.

## Two border shapes, because only two survive markdown

A **frame** is a top and a bottom line with no verticals: nothing has to line up down the page, so a proportional font cannot ragged it. A **divider** is a single line between sections.

Both are built as an anchor plus a repeating unit, which is the shape people actually make. The presets include one built from each of the two real posts this was designed against, plus clean, hearts and waves. Creators can paste their own.

## Three things handled so nobody has to think about them

- **Line breaks survive on HotAudio except around links**, so every link line is given a blank line either side.
- **Borders are kept on their own line** — some of the characters are right-to-left and would scramble anything sharing that line.
- **Pasted art is checked against the markdown that would eat it** — a line of dashes becomes a horizontal rule, `#` becomes a heading, backticks open a code block. The warning appears as you type rather than after posting.

The opening line sits in a code fence, which forces an even width; links never go inside one, since they stop working there.

A creator's chosen borders save to their profile (`postStyle`), so their posts look like theirs without setting it up each time.

## Testing

Rendered against a realistic entry: default frame and divider, the braille divider with no frame, section toggles, and the markdown-collision warning firing on a row of dashes. Link lines come out with blank lines around them; credits render from the catalogue's roles; TRT rides in the link text as it does in the Reddit generator.

## Not included

The Reddit generator is untouched. The engine is proven now, but retrofitting it means changing something in active use — better as its own step once this has been posted with for real.

The JOI divider preset is regenerated from the pattern rather than copied character-for-character. If the exact width matters, pasting it into the custom field and saving makes it permanent.

author: jkitchin
body:
Completes the #174 groundwork. **Stacked on #179**, and merges in #177's branch so the integration could actually be built and tested — so this diff also contains the kinetics merge. Once #177 and #178 land, this rebases down to just the two changes below.

## 1. A data-built rate law now survives a save

I told you in #179 that #177 and #179 would compose. **They didn't.** `mass_action_kinetics` made the rate law constructible from data, but `params_kwargs()` still handed `CSTRParams` a **closure**, and a closure can't be written to a file — so a reactor still refused to serialize. That was a real gap between two PRs that each looked complete.

The generated `rate_fn` now carries the specification that produced it, and the serializer writes *that* instead of the function:

```json
"rate_fn": {"$callable": {"factory": "mass_action_kinetics",
                          "attr": "rate_fn",
                          "kwargs": {"reactions": [...], "species_order": [...]}}}
```

Rebuilding calls the factory and takes the attribute back off it, returning the identical function — **a reloaded reactor solves to bit-identical results**. The protocol is general: any module can make its callables serializable by attaching `__difflow_spec__`.

## 2. `difflow.codegen` writes a flowsheet as runnable Python

```python
codegen.save_script(fs, "plant.py")
```

The other half of the round trip. An editor you can only *enter* is worse than none — the moment you want something the palette doesn't offer, you have to drop into Python and keep going. Build in a GUI, export a script, edit it, read it back through `serialize`.

Output is meant to be read, not just run:

```python
kinetics_reactor = mass_action_kinetics(reactions=[...], species_order=['water', 'ethanol'], reverse='error')
thermo_flash = IdealThermo({s: get_species_data(s) for s in ['water', 'ethanol']})

fs = Flowsheet(species_order=['water', 'ethanol'], ...)
fs.add_feed('feed', make_stream({'water': 1.0, 'ethanol': 0.1}, T=350.0, P=101325.0))
fs.add_unit(Unit('reactor', CSTR(CSTRParams(**kinetics_reactor.params_kwargs(), V=1.0, ...)), ['feed'], ['rx']))
```

My first version inlined the whole `mass_action_kinetics(...)` call into the `CSTRParams(...)` argument list. It ran, but produced a single 600-character line that also repeated every array the factory derives. Hoisting it and splatting `params_kwargs()` back is both readable and shorter — `stoich` and the order matrices don't appear at all.

## Two things the generator has to get right that JSON doesn't

Both were bugs I hit, both now have tests:

- **`repr` writes infinity as `inf`**, which is not a name in the generated module — the script failed on import. Numeric literals go through their own renderer emitting `float('inf')`.
- **Unused names must stay out of the import block**, or the header fills with every unit in the package.

## Consistent refusals

Both formats refuse exactly the same things: an unregistered operation, and a callable that doesn't record how it was built. A generated script that quietly dropped a rate law would still run, and would be a different model. `CodegenError` subclasses `SerializationError`, so either can be caught.

## Verification

`1462 passed, 2 skipped` — 65 new tests across the two modules. The load-bearing ones are that a **reloaded flowsheet** and a **generated script** each solve to bit-identical results; structure alone would be a trap, since the difference stays invisible until it matters.

## Where #174 stands

The library groundwork from the plan is done:

| | |
|---|---|
| declarative kinetics | #177 |
| core units registered + catalog | #178 |
| JSON round-trip | #179 |
| rate-law round-trip + codegen | this |

Remaining are the two UI-facing pieces — a local-server editor, and the publication export (a `vmap` sweep shipped as a self-contained page). Both now have the data model they need.

author: jjcm
body:
<!-- CURSOR_AGENT_PR_BODY_BEGIN -->
Three pieces of work: the hosted provider comes out of the CLI, the landing page stops showing numbers and shapes it cannot back up, and the site leaderboard sheds some decoration and a stat card.

---

# 1. Remove the hosted Makefaster provider from the CLI

The hosted provider served `stealth/ox-alpha` and `z-ai/glm-5.2:free` through `makefaster.dev`. Neither is a free model any more, so the row the picker listed first and pre-selected could only fail on its first completion. It is removed rather than repointed at a different model.

## What the CLI does now

The provider picker lists only the local agent CLIs that were actually detected — Cursor Agent, Claude Code, Codex — and nothing is offered without being found. On a machine with none of them installed, `missingCliGuidance` is now reachable and prints the three install commands instead of a hosted fallback:

```
makefaster could not find any supported agent CLI on this machine.

  Cursor Agent  curl https://cursor.com/install -fsS | bash
  Claude Code   curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash   (or: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code)
  Codex         npm install -g @openai/codex
```

`--cli makefaster` (and the `openrouter` / `hosted` aliases it answered to) is refused with the reason rather than falling through to a local CLI — silently running somebody's loop on an agent and an account they did not pick is worse than a one-line error:

```
x --cli makefaster is gone: makefaster no longer hosts a model of its own — use --cli cursor, claude, or codex.
```

An unrecognised value still reads as a typo: `--cli must be one of: cursor, claude, codex (got "gemini")`.

## What was removed

| | |
|---|---|
| `lib/detect.js` | the always-found `makefaster` entry, the `hosted` branch, and the `hosted`/`hostedModels`/`detail` report fields |
| `lib/models.js` | `HOSTED_MODELS` and `resolveHostedModel` |
| `lib/args.js` | the hosted aliases and every line of usage copy about a model needing no CLI, account, or key |
| `bin/makefaster.js` | `pickHostedModel`, `checkHostedModel`, and the hosted branches in the provider picker and `main` |
| `lib/session.js` | the `makefaster` runner, plus the `apiBase`/`plannedRuns` arguments only it used |
| `lib/agents/openrouter.js`, `lib/agents/tools.js` | deleted — the in-process agent loop and its toolset |
| `lib/thinkingTrace.js` | the `openai-message` reasoning extractor |
| `lib/invoke.js` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` from `NEVER_INJECTED_ENV`, which was there for the hosted credential boundary |

Local CLI detection, the per-CLI model pickers and their CursorBench ranking, and leaderboard/trace submission are untouched.

`test/openrouter.test.mjs` is deleted. The tests that pinned hosted behaviour now pin its absence: detection lists exactly `cursor, claude, codex` with no `hosted` flag on any report, the catalog exports no `HOSTED_MODELS` and offers no `ox-alpha`/`glm-5.2` id, `--cli makefaster` errors under every name it had, and `USAGE` may not mention a hosted model.

README's flow, the two `SKILL.md` files, and `env.example` said the hosted option came first, was pre-selected, and needed no account or key. That copy now describes the picker as it behaves.

**The backend proxy is left serving.** `POST /api/openrouter/v1/chat/completions`, its allowlist, and its rate limiter are unchanged — that is a deployed server surface, and removing it is a separate call. Its comments and docs now say that nothing in this repo calls it and that an unset `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is the expected state. Worth a follow-up if the endpoint should go too.

---

# 2. Landing page

## The specimen line credits @pwnies

[The specimen line reading + MADE BY @PWNIES +](https://cursor.com/agents/bc-9d4dec42-c26f-40c8-a8c2-b9c7a16d7fd9/artifacts?path=%2Fopt%2Fcursor%2Fartifacts%2Fscreenshots%2Fspecimen-line.png)

It read `Specimen No. 001` as a non-interactive span, and the whole line was `aria-hidden`. The credit is a real link to [x.com/pwnies](https://x.com/pwnies) now, so `aria-hidden` moves onto the two plus marks — they are the decoration, the credit is not — and the link picks up the hover underline and focus outline the rest of the site's links use. The mono, red, wide-tracked specimen look and the plus marks are unchanged.

## The metric arrowhead draws its whole chevron

[The annotation arrow before and after, at 12x and actual size](https://cursor.com/agents/bc-9d4dec42-c26f-40c8-a8c2-b9c7a16d7fd9/artifacts?path=%2Fopt%2Fcursor%2Fartifacts%2Fscreenshots%2Farrow-before-after.png)

The head was `M11.5 17.5 6.4 21.9l6.4 1.4`. Both arms were in the viewBox, so nothing was clipped — the problem was that the upper arm ran almost along the curve that feeds it and the curve painted straight over it. What reached the screen was one arm and a hook.

Both arms are now placed off the curve's own end tangent (`P3-P2` of the cubic), symmetric about it at 38° and equal length, which puts the upper arm clear of the curve instead of underneath it. The curve is byte-for-byte the same path. Round caps and joins finish the tip. Extreme points are x 7–12.9 and y 15.6–22.2, inside the 22×26 viewBox with room for the 1.3 stroke, so nothing depends on overflow.

## The averages band is live

[The averages band showing LCP -30%, TTI -20% and 3 sites from the live board](https://cursor.com/agents/bc-9d4dec42-c26f-40c8-a8c2-b9c7a16d7fd9/artifacts?path=%2Fopt%2Fcursor%2Fartifacts%2Fscreenshots%2Fband-live.png)

The band showed four hardcoded columns — LCP -38%, INP -27%, CLS -24%, TTFB -31% — under the claim "based on sites that have completed 5+ improvement cycles". Three of those metrics are not on the board at all: a submission carries LCP and TTI and nothing else, so INP, CLS and TTFB were numbers with no source, and the two that did exist were stale the moment they were typed.

It now reads `getSites()` and shows what the board actually holds: average LCP improvement, average TTI improvement, and the number of sites. No fourth metric is invented — submissions carry no Lighthouse performance score, so the band does not imply one. The screenshot above is a four-row stub board (one site measured both cold and warm at -40/-10, one cold at -20, one warm at -30) rendering as -30% / -20% / 3.

**Cold/warm duplicates.** A site is on the board once per load mode, so averaging the raw rows would weigh a site measured both ways twice as heavily as one measured once. `frontend/js/site-stats.js` collapses that to one run per site, preferring the cold load — the harder number, and the one the site leaderboard shows by default — and keeps a warm-only site rather than dropping it. The band's own copy states the choice instead of leaving it to be inferred.

**An empty board is a real state, not a failure.** The columns keep their frame and their baseline rule, print an en dash, and draw no bars, because a zero-height "after" bar beside a full "before" bar reads as a 100% improvement. A board that cannot be fetched leaves the dashes and says so.

[The band on an empty board: en dashes, zero sites, and a note that the board is still filling up](https://cursor.com/agents/bc-9d4dec42-c26f-40c8-a8c2-b9c7a16d7fd9/artifacts?path=%2Fopt%2Fcursor%2Fartifacts%2Fscreenshots%2Fband-empty.png)

The count column is not a before/after pair, so it prints one number rather than pretending to a baseline. Three metrics also needed the tablet breakpoint changed — three into two columns left an empty cell — so at ≤1100px the info panel takes its own row and the metrics share the next; at ≤720px they stack.

[The band stacked in a single column at 700px](https://cursor.com/agents/bc-9d4dec42-c26f-40c8-a8c2-b9c7a16d7fd9/artifacts?path=%2Fopt%2Fcursor%2Fartifacts%2Fscreenshots%2Fband-narrow.png)

---

# 3. Site leaderboard trims

[The site leaderboard: no ref tab, no eyebrow dots, a tight geo row, and four stat cards](https://cursor.com/agents/bc-9d4dec42-c26f-40c8-a8c2-b9c7a16d7fd9/artifacts?path

author: dmitry123
body:
## Why

`benches/README.md` advertised `fib(47)` at **484ns** for rWasm while the benchmark reported ~4.5µs. The VM had not regressed.

The table was measured in May 2025 against `benchmarks/bench.rs`, which built the store and engine **outside** `b.iter` — its 484ns row timed execution against an already-instantiated module. When the benchmark was rewritten for Criterion (`ece6e9ba`), the README was copied over verbatim while the harness moved instantiation **inside** the loop. The two have described different work ever since.

Verified by running the unmodified benchmark at `ece6e9ba` — the commit that introduced the table — and at `HEAD`, back to back on the same machine: **5.02µs** then, **4.53µs** now. `HEAD` is ~10% faster than the day the "484ns" table landed.

## What was actually slow

`wasm-ld` reserves a 1 MiB shadow stack by default, which reaches the module as a 16-page minimum linear memory. `fib` is pure integer arithmetic and never touches it, but every instantiation still allocated and zeroed that megabyte.

Phase breakdown before this change:

| Phase | Time |
|---|---|
| full iteration | 4.58 µs |
| `create_executor` only | 4.21 µs |
| `execute` only, reused executor | 0.31 µs |
| raw 1 MiB alloc + zero (baseline) | 4.09 µs |

## Changes

**`examples/fib/build.rs`** — link with `-zstack-size=0`, so the module declares a zero-page memory and instantiation allocates nothing. Cold instantiation plus execution: **4.5µs → 476ns**.

`.env_remove("CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS")` is load-bearing: Cargo hands build scripts an encoded copy that takes precedence over `RUSTFLAGS` in the inner build, so the flag is silently ignored without it.

**`benches/bench.rs`** — warm and cold variants for both backends. Both now meter fuel, so neither is credited for skipping the other's work (metering costs rWasm ~3–4%, measured). Fuel limit raised to `u64::MAX`: the warm loops never reset it, and the previous `1_000_000_000` against Wasmtime's 213 fuel/run would have hit `OutOfFuel` and panicked after ~4.7M iterations. The result is now asserted rather than merely unwrapped, since a warm executor carries guest state and silent drift would read as a speedup. Removed a commented-out wasmi block referencing a `../lib.wasm` and a `compile_wasmi_module` that do not exist.

**`benches/README.md`** — rewritten around the same split. Dropped the wasmi columns, the SP1 footnote and the decoding-cost projections; none are measured here. Corrected the host, which was inherited from the 2025 table.

## Results

`fib(43)`, Apple M5 Max:

| Backend | warm | cold |
|---|---|---|
| Native Rust | 10.5 ns | — |
| rWasm interpreter | 322 ns | 476 ns |
| Wasmtime (JIT) | 109 ns | 5.48 µs |

Wasmtime takes the warm row ~3x (JIT vs interpreter, expected). rWasm takes the cold row by an order of magnitude — an entire rWasm call costs less than Wasmtime's store construction.

## On warm benchmarks

The README documents why the warm row is sound here and not in general. `StrategyExecutor::execute` performs no reset. The interpreter's own value and call stacks are rebuilt per call, so those are never the issue — but guest state survives: mutable globals, linear memory, segment-drop flags, consumed fuel.

A guest that traps never restores its shadow stack pointer, and nothing resets that global:

```
clean warm runs        sp = 65536, 65536, 65536
a run that traps       Err(UnreachableCodeReached)
warm runs after that   sp = 65520, 65520, 65520   <- never recovers
```

`RwasmStore::reset(false)` plus re-running the entrypoint restores globals and re-applies data segments, but does not zero linear memory — bytes written outside a data segment survive. Building a fresh instance is the only clean path, which is what the cold row measures.

## Caveat

The cold row is a floor, not a typical figure: a real module declares real memory and pays to allocate and zero it. The README says so.

## Testing

Full suite passes, `cargo clippy --benches` and `cargo fmt --check` clean.

One pre-existing failure on `devel`, untouched by this PR: `max_stack_height_records_the_peak_not_the_current_height` (`tests/value-stack-api.rs:51`). Verified failing with the original `build.rs` in place.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Documentation**
  * Updated benchmark documentation to compare warm and cold execution paths across Native Rust, rWasm, and Wasmtime.
  * Added context on benchmark limitations and when warm execution results are applicable.

* **Tests**
  * Expanded benchmarks to cover cached and fresh execution scenarios.
  * Added result validation and updated execution metering for more reliable measurements.

* **Chores**
  * Optimized the Fibonacci example’s WebAssembly build configuration by removing unnecessary stack reservation.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

author: vasanthdev2004
body:
Patch release.

- **[#33](https://github.com/Vasanthdev2004/Game-Save-Genie/pull/33)** — autostart could fail at logon, or silently start nothing. The startup script was written as UTF-8, which Windows Script Host does not read. A UTF-8 BOM makes WSH refuse the file outright (`Invalid character`, 800A0408, line 1 char 1). Without a BOM it is read as the system ANSI codepage, which agrees with UTF-8 only while every character is ASCII — so a profile like `C:\Users\José` produced a startup entry pointing at a path that does not exist, and since the script opens with `On Error Resume Next`, it failed silently every logon with nothing logged. Now UTF-16LE with a BOM, verified against real `cscript`.
- **[#34](https://github.com/Vasanthdev2004/Game-Save-Genie/pull/34)** — adds `CLOUD_FORMAT.md`, documenting the cloud layout so something other than `gsg` can read and write it. Groundwork for [#32](https://github.com/Vasanthdev2004/Game-Save-Genie/issues/32), where the target device has 128 MB of RAM and cannot run Python.

## Who this matters to

Anyone whose Windows profile has a non-ASCII character has had broken autostart since the feature shipped, without any way to notice — the failure was silent by construction. 0.6.2 shipped with it.

## Changes here

`0.6.2` → `0.6.3` in `pyproject.toml` and `__init__.py`, plus the changelog section. The fixes themselves merged as #33 and #34.

Verified locally: `gsg --version` reports 0.6.3, 229 tests pass, ruff and mypy clean, `check_deps.py` confirms all 13 runtime dependencies declared.

The released crowdin.exe carried no VERSIONINFO resource at all, so Windows showed no publisher, product name or version in file properties. An unsigned PE with a blank version resource also feeds AV heuristics - 5.0.0 came back 1/68 on the Chocolatey virus scan.

Bun's --windows-* flags only work on a Windows host (they depend on Windows APIs), so the exe can no longer be cross-compiled on ubuntu. Build it once in a new win-binary job and reuse that artifact for the npm package, the release asset and the Inno Setup installer. Side benefit: the installer now ships the exact binary the release publishes instead of a separately compiled one.

Both Windows jobs assert the metadata is non-empty, so the flags cannot fall out of the build script unnoticed.

body:
## What this measures

W3.29 (`ad4d757`, #205) pinned the 13 shipped defaults. Its own handover named the gap this closes:

> the census measures whether a default is **PINNED**, not whether it is **ENFORCED** — recording `MaxBodyBytes` does not prove a 5MB body is rejected.

W3.29 mutated the **default** in `config.go`. This census mutates the **use site** in `cmd/docs/main.go` — the wire between a configured value and the component that enforces it.

## Result: 9 of 9 NOT ENFORCED, 0 ENFORCED

| ceiling | mutation | suite |
|---|---|---|
| AI rate 30/min | → 1e9 | GREEN |
| search rate 240/min (gates embed spend) | → 1e9 | GREEN |
| index rate 300/min (gates embed spend) | → 1e9 | GREEN |
| index burst 10 | → 1e9 | GREEN |
| index workers 4 | → 512 | GREEN |
| re-embed staleness 5s | → 0 | GREEN |
| /mcp body 4MB | → 1TB | GREEN |
| /v1 body 4MB | → 1TB | GREEN |
| import body 200MB | → 1TB | GREEN |

All 45 packages stayed green on every one. **Positive control** — breaking the cap comparison inside `internal/bodylimit`, a package that *is* tested — came back **RED**, so the nine greens were the product's and not the harness's.

## Why nothing saw it

`cmd/docs` has **no test files at all** (`go list` → `TestGoFiles=[]`), so all 750 lines of `main.go` are covered only by tests that read it as *source*. The `mainwiring` family does exactly that — and `internal/ratelimit/mainwiring_test.go` states its own boundary in its header: it **"CANNOT see a wrong argument."** It pins that `WithRateLimit(` is *called*; it cannot pin *which* limiter, and no sibling pins which *value* went into one. The argument is the half nobody was holding.

## What merges

One new test file. It records, per configured value, the consumers `main.go` hands it to — population **recomputed from the file on every run**, so a new configured value wired in without being recorded is a red rather than an omission.

**This changes no value and moves no ceiling.** Whether 30/min, 4MB or 200MB is the *right* number is a threshold on a spend path and is deliberately not taken here — the same posture `shipped_defaults_test.go` took about the same numbers.

Additive only: one new file, **zero deletions**, zero behaviour change.

## Controls — 15 rows, 0 miss

`~/talyvor-queue/w330-mainwiring-controls-c5j7.py`

- **C1–C9** — the nine mutations the census scored GREEN before this file existed; each is **RED** with it.
- **C10** — a wiring line deleted outright → RED.
- **C11 / C11b** — rule A: a new configured value wired in but unrecorded → RED.
- **C12** — vacuity: the census pointed at a file with no wiring → RED, because *a scanner that finds nothing agrees with any table*.
- **C13, C14 — inverted, must stay GREEN**: a comment naming a wiring call must not move the census (AST, not grep), and adding a log line must not red it. *A census that reds on correct code gets relaxed until it reds on nothing.*

### C11 caught a real hole in the first draft

`consumerOf` treated **every** unqualified call as a type conversion and walked past it, so a value handed to a local function was credited to whatever enclosed that call — and when that was a `slog` site, the value was **dropped from the census entirely**. Rule A stayed green with a configured value wired in and unrecorded: the exact failure rule A exists to prevent. Fixed by naming the conversions explicitly.

The same fix corrected a live mis-attribution: `cfg.ListenAddr` flows through `listenHostname()`, which the old walk skipped and credited to `customdomain.DomainRouter()`.

### The comparison is a multiset, not a set

`cfg.MaxBodyBytes` reaches `bodylimit.Middleware` **twice** (the `/mcp` group and the `/v1` group). A set-valued table still contains that label after one of the two is replaced by a literal — passing while half the service is uncapped. C7/C8 are the two halves.

## Gauntlet

Exact CI commands, real Postgres (`pgvector/pgvector:pg16`): `gofmt -l .` clean · `go vet ./...` clean · `go test -timeout 300s -race -count=1 ./...` → **45 packages ok, 0 FAIL**.

author: gigara
body:
> **Stacked on #2245**: this PR's base is that PR's branch, so the diff below is the update mechanism alone. Merge #2245 first, then retarget this PR to `main` (one click) and merge.

Lets a shipped Integrator update its bundled components — the Ballerina runtime, the JRE, ICP, and the six extensions — and the app itself, without waiting for a full product release.

## Shape

The client posts its inventory to `POST /api/v1/updates` and the **server decides** what to offer, composing each response from one cosign-signed source document per release. Rollout, entitlement and kill-switch decisions live server-side, changeable without shipping a client. A per-channel `index.json` maps a client-version selector (`5.1.x`, an exact version, a range) to the document that serves it — first match wins — so a 5.1 maintenance line and a 5.2 line coexist without either touching the other's document.

## Trust

Two things are signed, verified by different parties: the **source document** (checked by the update server) and a per-artifact **statement** binding `{id, version, sha256, sizeBytes, requires}` (checked by the client against a key pinned in `product.json` at build time). Signing the statement rather than the bytes is what stops a manipulated document offering an old, genuinely signed artifact under a new version label — and it is why the server can compose responses per client without ever holding the signing key. CI compares the pinned key against the signing key before every publish, since a mismatch would otherwise surface only as every client rejecting every artifact, after release.

On the machine: runtime components are staged and swapped at the next launch — the only moment nothing runs from the directories being replaced — and an activated runtime that keeps the app from booting is rolled back automatically after two failed starts. The app applies via Squirrel.Mac (macOS) or an in-place user-context MSI (Windows). No privilege elevation anywhere.

## Publishing

Opt-in by design: `build.yml` takes `publish_update_source` defaulting to **false**; only the Release workflow sets it (default true, switchable off) — so a nightly cannot claim a release line by accident. A separate `publish-components.yml` ships a component fix with no app build, tag or installers, in minutes. Both publishers share one index-upsert script (unreachable-entry and sequence-regression guards) and a per-channel concurrency group; sequences are UTC clock reads so the publishers never coordinate numbering. `promote-channel.yml` copies already-signed documents down the insider→beta→stable ladder, per line.

## Verified

On real hardware against a deployed server: discovery, download, statement verification, staging, activation and `${COMPONENT:*}` resolution against a live Ballerina process; three forged artifacts and a tampered document all refused; channel selection and insider→beta promotion; a component-only publish delivering an extension update with no app release. Windows in-place MSI apply and macOS Squirrel were verified under the earlier flow. Not yet exercised: Linux, and Windows against the server-decided flow.

## Review

Multi-round pre-PR review (three scoped manual reviewers + CodeRabbit, two rounds): 7 critical and ~15 warning findings fixed — among them server-supplied id/version path validation before any filesystem use, refusing HTTP redirects (which would have leaked the Authorization header and escaped the host allowlist), fail-closed verification when a required pinned key is unusable, and promotion aborting on transient read failures instead of rebuilding the target index. The verification round returned clean; remaining known risks (signing-key rotation → KMS, trust-on-publish for upstream artifacts, unenforced statement `sizeBytes`) are tracked in the threat model's risk registry.

## Secrets

`WSO2_UPDATE_URL`, `WSO2_UPDATE_PUBLIC_KEY`, `WSO2_UPDATE_ARTIFACTS_URL`, `AWS_UPDATE_S3_BUCKET`, `COSIGN_*`. All optional: without them the updater ships disabled rather than broken. The update server is deployed separately and is not in this repository.

author: ebarkhordar
body:
Fixes #407.

`.to_solver()` reads the system prompt and any prior turns out of Inspect AI's message state. Inspect AI types `ChatMessage.content` as `str | list[Content]`, and messages that Inspect AI itself builds carry the `str` form, so two paths were wrong.

**1. `chatlas/_chat.py:1137` set the system prompt to the message's repr.** `str(system_messages[0])` on a `ChatMessageSystem` gives `"id='...' content='You are terse.' source='input' metadata=None role='system'"`, complete with a per-run id. Now `system_messages[0].text`.

**2. `chatlas/_inspect.py:131,134,143` iterated `msg.content` directly.** With the `str` form that walks characters, so `"What is 2+2?"` became 12 single-character `ContentText` objects and `turn.text` came back as `'What[empty string]is[empty string]2+2?'`. Added a small `message_contents()` helper that normalizes to a list, mirroring the guard `.to_solver()` already applies to the user prompt at `chatlas/_chat.py:1152-1154`.

The existing round-trip tests could not see either one: `turn_as_inspect_messages()` always emits the `list` form, so they only ever exercise that branch.

## Verification

Clean `python:3.12-slim` container on Linux, `pip install -e .`, inspect-ai 0.3.260, Python 3.12.14. No network calls. Base commit `6e0671bce38bb0c5e2488ae9f59c85167d1a8fb6`.

Five new tests, one per scenario named above plus a control:

| | base | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| `TestStringMessageContent` + `TestSolverSystemPrompt` (6 tests) | **5 failed, 1 passed** | **6 passed** |
| `TestContentTranslation` + `TestExportEval*` (21 tests) | 21 passed | 21 passed |

The one test that passes on base is `test_list_content_still_works`, the control for the branch that was already correct.

`ruff check chatlas --config pyproject.toml` passes, and `pyright chatlas/_inspect.py` reports 0 errors. `pyright chatlas/_chat.py` reports only the two pre-existing unresolved `shiny` / `shinychat` imports, which are absent from my container rather than caused by this change.

I did not run the live legs (`test-live`) or anything needing a cassette that does not exist yet, so nothing here is a claim about a real provider round trip.

## Scope note

`TestSolverSystemPrompt` drives the real `solve()` body and subclasses `Chat` to intercept `chat_async`, so the solver runs end to end without a provider call. Happy to reshape that if you would rather it went through a cassette.

author: arkstack-dev
body:
Closes the distributed half of the v0.12 security-alert item.

## What changed

| Coordinate | From | To | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tools.jackson.core:*` | 3.1.1 | 3.2.2 | `exeris-kernel-bom` — distributed |
| `org.postgresql:postgresql` | 42.7.11 | 42.7.13 | `exeris-kernel-bom` — distributed |
| `at.yawk.lz4:lz4-java` | 1.10.2 | 1.11.2 | `exeris-kernel-bom` — distributed |
| `com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind` | 2.18.7 | 2.22.2 | `tools/jfr-reporter` — CI tooling |

The lz4 entry is the one worth naming: `at.yawk.lz4:lz4-java` is not declared anywhere: it reaches the tree only as a runtime transitive of `kafka-clients`, and it is this BOM entry that pinned it at the vulnerable version. Verified on the resolved tree, not from the property.

## Two corrections to the inherited framing

**The alert count describes `main`, not this line.** Dependabot scans the default branch, which still carries 0.11.0. Seven of the alerts it reports are against an `exeris-kernel-diagnostics-cli` that no longer matches its own description — the CLI's Jackson 2 was removed on `development/0.12.0` when the module moved to the kernel's Jackson 3. Those close on release integration and owe no bump here. What was genuinely open was the BOM and the reporter.

**`tools/jfr-reporter` stays on Jackson 2, deliberately.** The case for finishing the migration was that the distribution should not carry two Jackson generations — and it no longer does. The reporter has its own POM, inherits neither the parent nor the BOM, is outside the reactor, and is never deployed; only the CI JFR job builds and runs it. Rewriting a report writer whose output feeds that job, to remove a dependency no consumer resolves, trades real risk for no consumer benefit.

## Verification

- `mvn clean install`, full reactor, **no skip flags** → `BUILD SUCCESS`, so checkstyle (`validate`) and PMD (`verify`) both actually ran.
- `ExerisArchitectureTest` **13/13**, `KernelTierBanArchitectureTest` **5/5** — run because a version bump changes real transitives, not because a POM diff looked safe.
- `DiagnosticsCliShadedJarIT` **7/7** against the shaded jar under jackson 3.2.2.
- **The reporter was executed, not merely built**: shaded jar against a real JFR recording → 180 allocation events through the streaming generator, all five JSON artefacts written, exit 0. This is the check the earlier CLI regression taught, where a jar that assembled cleanly was executed nowhere in CI.
- Resolved tree confirms all three: `jackson-databind:3.2.2`, `lz4-java:1.11.2`, `postgresql:42.7.13`.

No SPI source changed, so the API-diff gate has nothing to compare; no ADR is owed — a version bump is not an architectural decision.

body:
Closes #246.

The example fixed in #236 bound the fixture to `alembic` and then called `alembic_runner` in
the body — an undefined name that raised `NameError` for anyone who copied it. It got past a
100%-coverage suite, `--doctest-modules`, and a docs build, because a `>>> def ...` body is
only *compiled*: doctest sees a function definition and never resolves the names inside it.
26 of the 60 examples under `src` are that shape, since they need a live fixture and a
database and so cannot carry doctest output. The instance was fixed; nothing stopped the
next one.

ruff does not lint code inside docstrings — checked against exactly that shape with
`--select F821`, which reports *All checks passed* — so this reads the examples out with
`doctest.DocTestFinder` and runs pyflakes over them, one test case per documented object.
It rides the existing suite rather than adding a CI job, so it runs in every matrix cell and
fails where a contributor is already looking.

### The seeding is the part that matters

An example may reference the object being documented and, for a method, its class. Anything
else it must import, because an example is something a reader copies into their own file.

The wider and more obvious choice — seed `vars(module)` — **makes this gate a no-op**:
`alembic_runner` is itself a module-level name in `plugin.fixtures`, so seeding the module
namespace finds zero problems in this package and would have let #236's bug through
unchanged. Measured both ways:

| Seeding | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `vars(module)` | 0 violations — the bug this exists for is invisible |
| documented object + its class | 3 violations, all real |

`test_the_check_sees_inside_a_def_body` pins that down against the historical bug's shape, so
a later "simplification" of the seeding fails loudly rather than silently disarming the check.

### The three violations it found are real

All in `alembic_config`'s docstring: the examples used `@pytest.fixture` and
`alembic.config.Config()` with no import line, so neither could be copied and run. Fixed by
importing what they use — which also documents what to import.

### Gates

- `make lint` clean (mypy included; the new module is annotated)
- `make test` 179 passed (150 + 28 documented objects + the check's own regression test), coverage unchanged at `885 stmts / 196 branches, 0 miss, 100%`
- `make deps`, `make docs` clean
- the floors job simulated locally, since this adds a dev dependency:
  `uv sync --all-groups --resolution lowest-direct` then
  `uv run --all-groups --resolution lowest-direct pytest src tests` → 178 passed, 1 skipped
  (the known `test_pyproject_toml` skip on alembic 1.9.0)

The `uv.lock` diff adds `pyflakes` only — re-locked with `--no-upgrade` so no other package
moves. The remaining churn in that file is uv rewriting dependency markers, the same
rewrite `f9bdc24` produced.

### Confirmed running in CI, not just locally

Read out of the job logs rather than inferred from the green tick: the parametrised cases and
`test_the_check_sees_inside_a_def_body` appear in **every** job — all eight `test` rows,
`lowest-deps`, and `cross-platform` on both Windows and macOS — at 179 passed per row.

author: camshaft
body:
Adds `cdz-smith verify-differential <FILE.sexp|SEED> [--store DIR] [--cdz PATH] [--oracle PATH]`: run ONE reproducer through the wasm backend + (if a `cdz` binary is discoverable) the rust backend, print each `Side` + the wasm-vs-rust `Diff`, and with `--oracle` also judge it via the Lean L2 oracle (a 1-trial batch).

The per-source counterpart to the `differential` / `lean-differential` sweeps — the tool for triaging a filed finding (or any program) WITHOUT re-running a whole campaign. The rust side is OPTIONAL (`cdz` + rlibs are a heavy separate build, and `lean-differential` findings only exercise wasm + Lean), so it still runs wasm + Lean when `cdz` is absent. Exits non-zero iff a disagreement fired.

Also extracts the `verify` source-resolution (file / seed / finding-name) into a shared `resolve_source` helper used by both `verify` and `verify-differential`. Feature-gated on `differential` (+ a stub under `not(feature)`), like the other backend subcommands.

Validated live on a filed finding: it revealed the actual wasm trap kind (`unreachable`) that a campaign aggregate hid — correcting a mis-triage. clippy (both feature configs) + fmt clean; 80 lib tests still green.

author: hanscanonico
body:
**What.** 34 bare `assert_ne(error, "")` sites across 14 suites now assert the literal string their authority returns, read off the `return "…"` in the `_error` body. Each touched suite carries `test_join_command.gd`'s header sentence.

`test_mission_triggers.gd`'s `test_unit_reached_refuses_an_unnamed_unit_or_no_ground` splits into three named cases — it set `tag = &"courier"` throughout, so `UnitReachedTrigger`'s unnamed-unit branch was never reached by the suite, and its three `assert_ne`s conflated no-ground / off-board / unknown-tag. Net +2 tests; nothing else moved.

**Why.** A bare `assert_ne` passes on *any* refusal, so a branch that started answering with its neighbour's message would keep the suite green.

**Finding (test fixed, code question left open).** `test_a_shapeless_save_is_refused` asserted that `CampaignSaveCodec.validate({"version": 1})` refuses. It does — but with `"save names no campaign"`, not a shape complaint: version 1 is a *legal older profile*, so that case tests the campaign-id check and not shapelessness. The test now asserts what the code actually says, with the reason on the assert. Open question for `core/` (deliberately not changed here): whether a v1 profile missing every later section should be refused as a shape at all, or whether the name check is the right and only door.

**How verified.** `make verify` green in the worktree (2237 tests, determinism golden reproduced). Every new literal grepped across `tests/` — no two suites state a message differently.

## Summary
Adds a configurable NixOS hardware module under `hardware.keyd` (`modules/nixos/hardware/keyd.nix`) supporting per-host activation, explicit device ID filtering, virtual keyboard libinput quirks for laptop palm rejection, and modular keymap feature toggles (CapsLock to Hangul and Copilot key to Meta layer).

## Key Changes
- **`modules/nixos/hardware/keyd.nix`**: Exposes `hardware.keyd` options (`enable`, `deviceIds`, `enableLibinputQuirk`, `remapCapsLockToHangul`, `remapCopilotToMeta`, `extraConfig`), automatically configuring `services.keyd.keyboards.default` and deploying `/etc/libinput/local-overrides.quirks` when active.
- **`modules/nixos/hardware/default.nix`**: Imports `./keyd.nix` into the shared hardware layer.
- **`tests/nixos/hardware-policy.nix`**: Adds test fixtures and assertions validating default disabled state, device ID matching in `[ids]`, layer remapping rules (`[main]` / `[control]`), libinput quirk deployment, and extraConfig injection.

## Verification
- `nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.hardware-policy --no-link`: PASSED
- `nix flake check`: PASSED (all checks and shell tests verified)

Closes #68

## Summary

Follow-up to #209. The "Beri Akses" (manual grant) UI and the new order/purchase system were two disconnected surfaces — an admin looking at a user's course access couldn't tell whether it came from a purchase, a manual grant, or free self-enroll, and had no visibility into that user's order history without switching tabs.

- Backend: `GET /api/admin/user-access` now also returns the user's order history (same effective-status logic as the Pesanan endpoints) and includes `courses.is_free` in the grantable-courses list.
- Frontend: the "Pengguna" tab's per-row modal and the standalone "Beri Akses" tab were two independent copies of the same markup — consolidated into one shared panel used by both. Now shows, per enrolled course: source (Dibeli / Diberi manual / Gratis) and status (Aktif / Dicabut / Kadaluarsa), plus an order-history table with a link into the existing order-detail modal. The manual-grant dropdown labels each course Gratis/Berbayar/Belum ditentukan so an admin can't accidentally hand out free access to a paid course without noticing.

## Validation
Seeded all three enrollment sources (purchase w/ linked order, admin_grant + revoked, self_enroll) against a local Postgres and confirmed the endpoint response shape matches what the new UI renders. `node --check` clean on both the backend route and the extracted admin.html inline script.

## Not implemented
No new tables/infra — pure consolidation of existing data already returned by Phase 1/2 endpoints.

##### Features and enhancements

- Added a balanced query planner ([#​5501](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5501)).
- Added symbol-ref tree support across the read path: a new `symbolref` model package, production and aggregation in symdb and the query backend, and resolution in the frontend after the final merge ([#​5321](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5321), [#​5322](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5322), [#​5334](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5334)).
- Made experimental asynchronous queries resumable ([#​5442](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5442)).
- Allowed compaction to read block metadata from object storage, adding the `metadata_source` and `metadata_fetch_timeout` options ([#​5427](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5427)).
- Improved debuginfod client resilience and observability in the symbolizer, adding the `resolve_timeout` option ([#​5449](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5449)).
- Added SDK scope usage tracking to the distributor ([#​5366](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5366)).

- Improved metastore and compaction performance by scanning block bounds before decoding and avoiding deep label clones when building block indexes ([#​5407](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5407), [#​5398](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5398)).
- Reduced allocations in timeseries build and merge ([#​5311](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5311)).

##### Bug fixes

- Stopped a single bad DLQ object from blocking metastore recovery ([#​5371](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5371)).
- Disabled raft pipeline replication in the metastore ([#​5518](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5518)).
- Fixed a double prefix on metastore index cache and DLQ metrics ([#​5543](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5543)).
- Allowed the segment writer shard shuffle table to grow past 4096 entries ([#​5519](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5519)).
- Served profile-type Series queries from metadata when the selector is empty ([#​5483](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5483)).
- Used `raft_log.CompactionJobStatusUpdate` instead of `metastorev1.CompactionJobStatusUpdate` in compaction ([#​5465](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5465)).
- Keyed adaptive placement distribution stats by tenant and dataset ([#​5450](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5450)).
- Collapsed stripped profiles to a single sample in the distributor ([#​5409](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5409)).
- Treated a JFR profile size limit of 0 as unlimited ([#​5502](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5502)).
- Excluded the pre-window boundary point from `profilecli` query top totals ([#​5359](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5359)).
- Pointed v2 dashboard event annotations at the Alloy events stream ([#​5499](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5499)).
- Fixed the missing namespace in Helm discovery RBAC objects ([#​5447](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5447)).

##### Security updates

- Updated Go to 1.25.13 ([#​5520](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5520)).
- Updated `go.etcd.io/etcd/client/pkg/v3` to v3.6.14 ([#​5526](https://redirect.github.com/grafana/pyroscope/pull/5526)).
